title: Finite-temperature mass gap and quench dynamics of mobile impurities in a Fermi gas
abstract: Recently, a mass-gap description of mobile impurities in a Fermi gas was introduced, which connects Anderson's orthogonality catastrophe for static impurities to the quasiparticle picture of Fermi polarons through a recoil-induced energy gap in the fermionic dispersion. That description, however, was restricted to zero temperature and did not address dynamics. Here we generalize the mass-gap model to finite temperature by combining the Lee--Low--Pines transformation with a self-consistent Hartree--Fock decoupling of the recoil-induced interaction, and we study the quench dynamics within this framework using the functional-determinant approach. At finite temperature the effective mass gap obeys the self-consistency equation $Δ(T)=2U_F\tanh[Δ(T)/4k_B T]$, with $U_F=k_F^2/2M$ and $M$ the impurity mass. This equation admits a nonzero solution below the characteristic temperature $T^*=U_F/(2k_B)$ and closes as $(T^*-T)^{1/2}$. We identify this closing as the mean-field signature of the thermal melting of the polaron and molecule quasiparticles. Computing the Ramsey response $S(t)$ after a sudden quench of the impurity--fermion interaction, we find that its long-time oscillations---quantum beats between the bound and in-gap states---disappear precisely above $T^*$. Our work ties the thermodynamic and dynamical fingerprints of polaron formation to a single temperature-dependent mean-field parameter.
summary: This theoretical work extends the description of impurities in a Fermi gas to finite temperatures by deriving a self-consistent equation for the effective mass gap $\Delta(T)$. The key finding is that the gap closes at a characteristic temperature $T^*$, signaling the thermal melting of quasiparticles. This thermodynamic crossover is mirrored dynamically by the disappearance of long-time quantum oscillations in the system's Ramsey response above $T^*$.
main_problem: The paper generalizes the mass-gap description of mobile impurities in a Fermi gas from zero temperature to finite temperature, and studies the resulting quench dynamics.
main_result: The effective mass gap closes at a characteristic temperature $T^*$, which is identified as the mean-field signature of the thermal melting of polaron and molecule quasiparticles. Furthermore, long-time quantum beats in the Ramsey response disappear precisely above $T^*$.
method: The study combines the Lee–Low–Pines transformation with a self-consistent Hartree–Fock decoupling to derive the finite-temperature gap equation, and uses the functional-determinant approach to compute quench dynamics.
model_or_system: The system consists of a single impurity of mass $M$ interacting via a contact interaction with a noninteracting Fermi sea of host fermions. The model is analyzed using a mean-field Hamiltonian derived from the full interaction.
key_observables: Effective mass gap $\Delta(T)$, Ramsey response $S(t)$, and the quasiparticle weight $Z$.
important_parameters: Characteristic temperature $T^* = U_F / (2k_B)$, Fermi momentum $k_F$, and the impurity mass $M$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Hartree–Fock decoupling, which is treated as a Gaussian (quasifree) approximation for the interacting system.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the mass-gap dispersion at different temperatures, showing the gap closing at $T^*$, and plot the Ramsey response $|S(t)|$ which exhibits oscillations for $T < T^*$ and decays monotonically for $T > T^*$.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the finite-temperature self-consistency equation for the mass gap $\Delta(T)$ and its relation to $T^*$. It then applies the functional-determinant approach to calculate the time evolution of the system overlap, $S(t)$, demonstrating the temperature dependence of the quantum beats.
why_interesting: The work provides a unified, mean-field framework to connect the thermodynamic signature (gap closing) with the dynamic signature (loss of quantum beats) of quasiparticle thermal melting in a Fermi gas, which is highly relevant for understanding strongly interacting quantum gases.
